set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set1.q: A 70-year-old man has a wandering atrial pacemaker. How many P wave shapes define it?
opts: At least two
Two shapes is not enough; a wandering atrial pacemaker needs at least three competing atrial sites and P wave shapes.
Exactly one
One P wave shape means one pacemaker, the sinus node; a wandering pacemaker shows at least three.
At least three
Correct. At least three different areas of the atria compete to be the pacemaker, so there are P waves of at least three different morphologies.
None visible
No visible P waves fits atrial fibrillation or a junctional rhythm; a wandering pacemaker has P waves of three shapes.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 11, 12

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set1.q: A 79-year-old woman is suspected of idioventricular rhythm. Which combination defines it?
opts: Irregular, narrow, no P waves
An irregular narrow rhythm without P waves suggests atrial fibrillation; idioventricular rhythm is regular and wide.
Regular, narrow, inverted P
Regular, narrow complexes with inverted P waves are junctional; idioventricular rhythm is wide with no P waves.
Regular, wide, no P waves
Correct. Idioventricular rhythm is a regular wide-complex rhythm (QRS longer than 0.12 seconds) with no detectable P waves, at 20 to 40 per minute.
Regular, wide, upright P
Upright P waves married to wide complexes would be a sinus rhythm with abnormal conduction, not idioventricular.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 75, 76

set1.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set1.q: A 45-year-old woman notices skipped beats; her strip is shown. What are the early beats?
opts: Premature ventricular complexes
Premature ventricular complexes are wide, with no P wave and an opposite-direction T wave; these early beats are narrow with a P wave.
Premature junctional complexes
A premature junctional complex has no P wave, an inverted one or one after the QRS; these early beats have an upright P of new shape.
Junctional escape beats
Escape beats come late, after a pause; these beats come early, before the next expected beat.
Premature atrial complexes
Correct. The early beats are narrow and each has its own P wave, shaped differently from the sinus P waves: premature atrial complexes.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 6, 7
set1.alt: Lead II strip with narrow complexes; some beats arrive early, each with a small wave before it that differs in shape from the others.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set1.q: A 41-year-old woman has an isolated premature junctional complex on a routine strip. What is its clinical significance?
opts: None, in isolation
Correct. Premature junctional complexes come from increased automaticity of the junction, and isolated ones have no clinical significance.
A run of tachycardia
A single beat is not a run; isolated premature junctional complexes have no clinical significance.
Sinus node failure
A premature beat comes early from increased junctional automaticity; sinus failure produces late escape beats.
Imminent cardiac arrest
Imminent arrest is suggested by a very slow agonal ventricular rhythm; an isolated junctional premature beat is benign.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 50

set1.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
set1.q: An 80-year-old woman has a junctional escape beat on her strip. When does such a beat occur?
opts: When junctional automaticity rises
Increased junctional automaticity produces early beats, premature junctional complexes; escape beats follow sinus failure.
When the sinus node fails or slows
Correct. Junctional escape beats occur when the sinoatrial node fails to fire or fires too slowly, so the junction steps in.
When the ventricles fire early
Early ventricular firing is a premature ventricular complex; a junctional escape beat answers a failing sinus node.
When an atrial circuit reenters
Atrial reentry causes flutter; escape beats appear when the sinus node fails or slows.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 52

set1.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set1.q: A 61-year-old man's strip is shown. What pattern do his premature beats follow?
opts: Bigeminy
Correct. A premature beat occurs every other beat, normal then premature, normal then premature: bigeminy.
Trigeminy
Trigeminy is a premature beat every third beat (two normal, one early); here every other beat is early.
Quadrigeminy
Quadrigeminy is every fourth beat premature; here the early beat alternates with each normal one.
A couplet
A couplet is two premature beats in a row; here single early beats alternate with normal ones.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 8
set1.alt: Two rhythm strips on green grid paper with narrow complexes arriving in close pairs separated by longer gaps.

set1.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set1.q: A 46-year-old woman's strip is shown; the arrow points to a deflection after one QRS. What is that early beat?
opts: A premature atrial complex
A premature atrial complex has an early upright P wave before its QRS; here the P falls after it.
A premature ventricular complex
A premature ventricular complex is wide with an opposite-direction T wave; this early beat is narrow.
A ventricular escape complex
A ventricular escape complex is wide and late; this beat is narrow and early.
A premature junctional complex
Correct. The early narrow beat has its P wave after the QRS (a retrograde P wave), which places its origin in the atrioventricular junction.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 50, 51
set1.alt: Green grid strip of narrow complexes; an arrow below one early beat points to a small notch just after its complex.

set1.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
set1.q: An 82-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the wide beat?
opts: A premature ventricular complex
A premature ventricular complex is wide but early; this wide beat comes late, after a long gap.
A junctional escape beat
A junctional escape beat is late but usually narrow; this late beat is wide.
A ventricular escape complex
Correct. The wide beat comes late, after the point where the next R wave was expected: a ventricular escape complex, as both nodes failed to pace.
A premature atrial complex
A premature atrial complex is early and narrow with its own P wave; this beat is late and wide.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 74
set1.alt: Strip of narrow complexes with one longer gap, ended by a single broad complex with an opposite-direction wave, then narrow beats resume.

set1.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
set1.q: A 77-year-old man's rate is 150 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia is regular with one sinus P wave shape; here the rhythm is irregular and the P waves vary.
Atrial flutter
Atrial flutter shows a regular sawtooth baseline instead of P waves; here separate P waves of differing shapes appear.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Correct. An irregular rhythm over 100 per minute with P waves of at least three shapes married to narrow complexes is multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Wandering atrial pacemaker
A wandering atrial pacemaker is the same rhythm under 100 per minute; at 150 it is multifocal atrial tachycardia.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 17, 18, 21, 22
set1.alt: Small lead II strip of very rapid narrow complexes at uneven spacing with small waves of varying shape between them.

set1.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
set1.q: A 78-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Atrial flutter
Flutter shows an organized sawtooth baseline; this baseline is chaotic and the spacing unpredictable.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. Narrow complexes at irregularly irregular intervals over a disorganized baseline with no P waves (fibrillatory waves only) is atrial fibrillation.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular too, but has distinct P waves of three shapes; here there are none.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia keeps a normal P wave before every QRS; here no P waves can be found.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 32, 33, 34, 35
set1.alt: Pink grid strip of narrow complexes at unpredictable spacing, with a wavy, shapeless baseline and no distinct waves before them.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set1.q: A 49-year-old woman is told her premature beats come in a trigeminal pattern. Which premature beats can form such patterns?
opts: Ventricular only
Premature ventricular complexes do form these patterns, but so do atrial and junctional ones.
Atrial only
Atrial bigeminy and trigeminy exist, but junctional and ventricular premature beats follow the same patterns.
All three types
Correct. Premature atrial, junctional and ventricular complexes can all come in bigeminy, trigeminy and quadrigeminy.
Escape beats only
Escape beats come late, after a pause; the patterns describe premature beats of any origin.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 73

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set1.q: A 74-year-old woman has frequent, grouped premature ventricular complexes. What can they do to her circulation?
opts: Raise cardiac output
Early ventricular beats come before the ventricles fill; frequent or grouped ones reduce output.
Leave output unchanged
Isolated ones may be harmless, but frequent or grouped premature ventricular complexes reduce cardiac output.
Reduce cardiac output
Correct. Frequent premature ventricular complexes, especially grouped ones, can cause a reduction in cardiac output.
Improve atrial filling
Ectopic ventricular beats do nothing for atrial filling; frequent ones reduce cardiac output.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 70

set1.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
set1.q: A 71-year-old woman's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Supraventricular tachycardia
The reentry tachycardia called supraventricular tachycardia has no visible atrial waves; this baseline is a sawtooth of flutter waves.
Atrial flutter
Correct. Regularly spaced narrow complexes ride on a repeating pointed sawtooth baseline (flutter waves at an atrial rate of about 300): atrial flutter.
Atrial fibrillation
Fibrillation is irregularly irregular with a disorganized baseline; this strip is regular with an organized sawtooth.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia has a single inverted P wave per QRS; here several flutter waves fill each interval.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 27, 28, 29
set1.alt: Long rhythm strip of narrow spikes with a repeating pointed zigzag baseline between them, the spikes evenly spaced.

set1.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
set1.q: A 34-year-old man's rate is 160 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Supraventricular tachycardia
Correct. A regular narrow-complex tachycardia over 150 per minute with retrograde P waves after the QRS (an RP interval rather than a PR) is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; this tachycardia is perfectly regular with a notch after each QRS.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with P waves of three shapes; this rhythm is regular with one notch after each QRS.
Atrial flutter
Flutter shows a sawtooth of flutter waves between complexes; here only a small notch follows each QRS.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 40, 43, 44
set1.alt: Gray grid strip with a faint watermark, showing very rapid, evenly spaced narrow complexes with small notches at their ends.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set1.q: A 22-year-old marathon runner's rate is 190 per minute (normal 60 to 100), with an upright P wave before every QRS. What is the rhythm?
opts: Supraventricular tachycardia
The reentry tachycardia called supraventricular tachycardia has no visible P waves (or retrograde ones); upright P before each QRS is sinus.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia needs P waves of three shapes and is irregular; one upright P shape is sinus.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia has inverted, hidden or retrograde P waves; an upright P before each QRS is sinus.
Sinus tachycardia
Correct. The rate does not determine the rhythm: normal P waves married to every QRS make it sinus, so this is sinus tachycardia, even at 190.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 40

set1.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set1.q: A 72-year-old man's strip is shown, with a short run of consecutive wide beats. What does the run represent?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia
Correct. Three or more consecutive premature ventricular complexes at a fast rate are ventricular tachycardia; a brief run like this one is nonsustained and needs evaluation.
A ventricular couplet
A couplet is only two premature ventricular complexes in a row; this run is six wide beats long.
Ventricular bigeminy
Bigeminy alternates single wide beats with normal ones; here the wide beats run back to back.
Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm is a slow escape rhythm of 20 to 40 per minute; this is a fast run of ectopic beats.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 70, 71
set1.alt: Strip with a few narrow beats, one broad beat, then a rapid run of six broad complexes before narrow beats return.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set1.q: A 62-year-old woman's rate is 70 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
The escape rhythm runs 40 to 60 per minute; this junctional rhythm at 70 is accelerated.
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm is wide with no P waves; these complexes are narrow.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Correct. Inverted P waves married to narrow QRS complexes with a short PR at 70 per minute make an accelerated junctional rhythm (60 to 100).
Normal sinus rhythm
A sinus rhythm at 70 would have upright P waves and a normal PR, not inverted P waves with a short PR.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 59, 62, 63
set1.alt: Gray grid strip with regularly spaced narrow complexes, each followed by a tall rounded wave.

set1.io: Compare and contrast junctional and idioventricular rhythms
set1.q: A 73-year-old man has a regular escape rhythm with no P waves. Which feature best separates junctional from idioventricular origin?
opts: The QRS width
Correct. Junctional rhythms travel down the normal pathway and are most commonly narrow, while idioventricular complexes are wide, longer than 0.12 seconds.
The regularity
Both rhythms are regular, so regularity does not separate them; QRS width does.
The P wave shape
Neither shows upright sinus P waves, and here none are visible; the QRS width is the clue.
The T wave height
T wave height is not a criterion for either; a narrow QRS points to the junction, a wide one to the ventricles.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 54, 76

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set1.q: A 67-year-old man's flutter ratio is unclear. How are the flutter waves counted?
opts: Count QRS complexes for six seconds
That gives the ventricular rate, not the flutter ratio; the ratio comes from counting troughs between QRS complexes.
Count troughs to the next QRS
Correct. Draw a line through the peaks of the flutter waves and count the troughs until the next QRS complex; that number sets the ratio.
Measure the PR interval
Flutter has no PR interval, because there are no P waves; count the flutter-wave troughs to the next QRS.
Divide 300 by the boxes
That is the 300 rate method; the flutter ratio comes from counting troughs between QRS complexes.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 26, 27

set1.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
set1.q: A 70-year-old man's rate is 50 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
Correct. A regular rhythm of 40 to 60 per minute with inverted P waves just before narrow QRS complexes and a short PR is a junctional escape rhythm.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Accelerated junctional rhythm has the same look at 60 to 100 per minute; at 50 it is a junctional escape rhythm.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia has upright P waves with a normal PR; inverted P waves with a short PR are junctional.
Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm is wide with no P waves at 20 to 40; these complexes are narrow.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 54, 55, 56
set1.alt: Rhythm strip with regularly spaced narrow complexes, each preceded closely by a small downward deflection.

set1.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set1.q: A 70-year-old man's strip is shown; two consecutive wide beats are circled. What do they show?
opts: A multifocal couplet
Correct. Two premature ventricular complexes in a row make a couplet, and their different shapes mean different ventricular foci: multifocal.
A unifocal couplet
Unifocal premature ventricular complexes share one shape from one focus; the two circled beats look different.
A unifocal triplet
A triplet is three in a row; the circle holds two beats of different shapes.
Ventricular bigeminy
Bigeminy alternates single premature beats with normal ones; here two wide beats come back to back.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 70, 71
set1.alt: Two-lead strip of narrow beats; a circle surrounds two consecutive broad complexes of different shapes.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set1.q: A 72-year-old woman's rate is 65 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm runs 20 to 40 per minute; at 65 the wide rhythm is accelerated.
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
Correct. Regular wide complexes with no P waves at 65 per minute fall in the accelerated idioventricular range of 40 to 100.
Normal sinus rhythm
A sinus rhythm would have upright P waves married to each QRS; here the complexes are wide with no P waves.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
The accelerated junctional rhythm is usually narrow; wide complexes with no P waves are ventricular.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 81, 84, 85
set1.alt: Blue grid strip with regularly spaced broad complexes, each followed by an opposite-direction wave, nothing between them.

set1.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
set1.q: A 79-year-old woman's atria are fibrillating. What does she lose?
opts: All ventricular filling
Seventy to 80 percent of ventricular filling is passive and continues; what is lost is the atrial kick.
Ventricular contraction
The ventricles still contract, at an irregular rate; what fibrillating atria lose is their own kick.
Atrioventricular conduction
Impulses still reach the ventricles irregularly through the node; the lost function is the atrial kick.
The atrial kick
Correct. In atrial fibrillation the atria quiver rather than contract, so the atrial kick (contraction) is lost; most ventricular filling is passive and continues.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 32

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set1.q: A 75-year-old man's strip is shown; the flutter waves are constant but the R to R intervals vary. How should it be documented?
opts: Flutter with 2:1 conduction
A fixed 2:1 ratio would give evenly spaced QRS complexes; here the spacing changes, so the conduction is variable.
Atrial fibrillation
Fibrillation has no organized waves; this baseline keeps its regular flutter waves, only the conduction varies.
Flutter with 4:1 conduction
A fixed ratio of any number gives a regular rhythm; unequal R to R intervals mean variable conduction.
Flutter with variable conduction
Correct. When the ratio of flutter waves to QRS complexes keeps changing, the rhythm is irregular and is documented as atrial flutter with variable conduction.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 25, 30, 31
set1.alt: Gray grid strip of four narrow complexes at unequal spacing, with a continuous rounded zigzag baseline between them.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set1.q: A 66-year-old man's lead II strip is shown; his P waves are inverted. Why?
opts: The sinus node fires early
An early sinus beat keeps an upright P in lead II; inversion means the atria are activated from below.
The ventricles fire first
Ventricles depolarizing first put the P wave after the QRS; inversion itself comes from bottom-up atrial activation.
Flutter waves replace them
Flutter waves form a continuous sawtooth; these are single inverted P waves from a junctional impulse.
The atria depolarize from below
Correct. A junctional impulse travels up into the atria and depolarizes them from the bottom up, away from positive lead II, so the P waves are inverted.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 47
set1.alt: Lead II strip of regularly spaced narrow complexes, each preceded closely by a small downward deflection, one drawn in red.

set1.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman's rate is 65 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Wandering atrial pacemaker
Correct. P waves of at least three shapes, each married to its QRS, an irregular rhythm and a rate under 100 make a wandering atrial pacemaker.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia needs a rate over 100 per minute; at 65 this is a wandering atrial pacemaker.
Premature atrial complexes
Premature atrial complexes are occasional early beats in an otherwise sinus rhythm; here the P wave shape keeps changing.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm is regular with one P wave shape; here it is irregular with several.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 11, 15, 16
set1.alt: Wide pink grid strip with deep narrow complexes at uneven spacing; the small waves in front of them change shape.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set1.q: A 67-year-old man's rate is 90 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm is the same wide rhythm at only 20 to 40 per minute; at 90 it is accelerated.
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
Correct. A regular, wide-complex rhythm with no P waves at 40 to 100 per minute is accelerated idioventricular rhythm.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Accelerated junctional rhythm is usually narrow, with inverted or hidden P waves; these complexes are wide.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is a narrow rhythm over 100 per minute; this is a wide rhythm at 90.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 81, 82, 83
set1.alt: Gray grid strip with regularly and fairly closely spaced broad complexes and no waves between them.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set1.q: A 33-year-old man's regular narrow tachycardia is shown; the highlighted notch ends each QRS. What is the notch?
opts: A true S wave
A true S wave is part of ventricular depolarization; this notch is a retrograde P wave buried at the end of the QRS.
A buried retrograde P wave
Correct. In the typical form, retrograde P waves are buried at the end of the QRS complex; these are called pseudo S waves.
A flutter wave
Flutter waves form a continuous sawtooth between complexes; here a single notch ends each QRS.
A fibrillatory wave
Fibrillatory waves are chaotic baseline activity in atrial fibrillation, not a repeating notch on a regular rhythm.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 39
set1.alt: Rhythm strip of tall, evenly spaced narrow complexes; a yellow circle highlights the small notch at the end of each one.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set1.q: A 53-year-old woman's atrioventricular node delays each impulse. Which zone slows conduction and can serve as the backup pacemaker?
opts: The transition zone
The transition zone receives the impulse from the sinus node and is arrhythmogenic; the slowing and backup role belong to the compact zone.
The compact zone
Correct. The compact zone, the core of the node, slows conduction to allow atrial contraction and ventricular filling, and resembles the sinus node anatomically.
The trigger zone
The trigger zone fires the signal down the His bundle; slowing and backup pacing are the compact zone's.
Bachmann's bundle
Bachmann's bundle conducts between the atria, outside the node; the compact zone slows conduction.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set1.q: A 69-year-old woman's strip shows P waves of three different shapes. What separates multifocal atrial tachycardia from a wandering atrial pacemaker?
opts: Regular R to R intervals
Both are irregular, because the pacemaker site keeps shifting; only the rate separates them.
Absent P waves
Both show P waves of at least three shapes; the difference is a rate over 100 per minute.
Wide QRS complexes
Either may have narrow or wide QRS complexes; the rate over 100 per minute is what separates them.
A rate over 100 per minute
Correct. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is exactly a wandering atrial pacemaker except that the rate is over 100 per minute.
set1.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 12, 17, 18

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set2.q: A 45-year-old man's rate is 110 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia has upright sinus P waves with a normal PR; the short-PR inverted P waves are junctional.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Accelerated junctional rhythm stops at 100 per minute; over 100 it is junctional tachycardia.
Junctional tachycardia
Correct. A regular junctional rhythm with inverted P waves, a short PR and narrow QRS complexes over 100 per minute is junctional tachycardia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three P wave shapes; this rhythm is regular with one.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 64, 65, 66
set2.alt: Pink grid strip with closely spaced narrow complexes, each followed by a small rounded wave.

set2.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
set2.q: A 79-year-old woman has ventricular escape complexes. Which failure produces them?
opts: Sinus node firing early
An early sinus beat would be narrow with a normal P; ventricular escape answers failure of both nodes.
Both nodes failing to pace
Correct. Ventricular escape complexes come late, when the sinoatrial node and the atrioventricular node both fail to act as the pacemaker.
An irritable ventricular focus
An irritable focus firing early gives premature ventricular complexes; escape complexes come late after nodal failure.
A reentry loop in the atrium
Atrial reentry produces flutter; ventricular escape follows failure of both the sinus and atrioventricular nodes.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 74

set2.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set2.q: A 52-year-old man's strip is shown; the arrows mark two beats. What are the marked beats?
opts: Premature ventricular complexes
A premature ventricular complex would be wide with no P wave; the marked beats are narrow.
Junctional escape beats
An escape beat arrives late, after a pause; the marked beats come early.
Sinus exit block
Sinus exit block leaves a gap with no beat at all; here extra beats arrive early.
Premature atrial complexes
Correct. Each marked beat comes early with a narrow QRS and a P wave of different shape: a premature atrial complex, from an atrial site outside the sinus node.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 6, 7
set2.alt: Rhythm strip of regularly spaced narrow complexes; two downward arrows mark beats that arrive sooner than expected.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set2.q: A 78-year-old woman's rate is 40 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
A junctional escape rhythm is usually narrow at 40 to 60 per minute; these complexes are wide with no P waves.
Idioventricular rhythm
Correct. A regular, wide-complex rhythm of 20 to 40 per minute with no P waves is idioventricular rhythm: the Purkinje network is pacing.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast run of wide complexes; this wide rhythm is slow and steady, so the Purkinje network is pacing.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia has upright P waves married to each QRS; here there are no P waves and the complexes are wide.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 75, 76, 77, 78
set2.alt: Pink grid strip with four widely spaced broad complexes, each followed by a wave in the opposite direction, and no waves between them.

set2.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set2.q: A 63-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the early beat?
opts: Premature atrial complex
A premature atrial complex is narrow with its own early P wave; this beat is wide with no P wave.
Premature ventricular complex
Correct. The early beat is wide and bizarre, with no P wave, and its T wave points opposite to the QRS: a premature ventricular complex.
Premature junctional complex
A premature junctional complex is narrow; this early beat is wide and deep.
Ventricular escape complex
A ventricular escape complex is wide but late, after a pause; this one comes early.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 69, 70
set2.alt: Pink grid strip of narrow complexes with small rounded waves; one early beat is a deep, broad downward complex followed by an upright wave.

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set2.q: A 59-year-old man has a regular narrow tachycardia at 150 per minute (normal 60 to 100). Which finding would make it atrial flutter rather than the reentry tachycardia?
opts: Sawtooth flutter waves
Correct. Atrial flutter (often 2:1, about 150 per minute) shows sawtooth flutter waves; the reentry tachycardia has no visible P waves or only retrograde ones.
No visible P waves
No visible P waves fits the reentry tachycardia, not flutter.
A regular R to R
Both rhythms can be regular; the sawtooth flutter waves are what identify flutter.
A narrow QRS
Both are supraventricular and narrow; the sawtooth identifies flutter.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 24, 27, 40

set2.io: Compare and contrast junctional and idioventricular rhythms
set2.q: Two patients each have a regular rhythm at 80 per minute (normal 60 to 100) with no P waves; one has wide complexes. What is the wide one?
opts: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
Correct. A wide, regular rhythm with no P waves at 40 to 100 per minute is accelerated idioventricular rhythm; the narrow one is accelerated junctional rhythm.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Accelerated junctional rhythm runs 60 to 100 per minute but is usually narrow; that describes the other patient.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is over 100 per minute and narrow; this wide rhythm at 80 is ventricular.
Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm is wide but only 20 to 40 per minute; at 80 it is the accelerated form.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 59, 81

set2.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set2.q: A 58-year-old man's strip is shown; the arrows mark two beats. What are the marked beats?
opts: Premature junctional complexes
Correct. Each marked beat comes early with a narrow QRS and no P wave in front of it: a premature junctional complex.
Premature atrial complexes
A premature atrial complex has its own early P wave of new shape; the marked beats have none.
Premature ventricular complexes
A premature ventricular complex is wide; the marked beats are as narrow as the others.
Junctional escape beats
Junctional escape beats come late, after a pause; the marked beats arrive early.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 50
set2.alt: Lead II rhythm strip of narrow complexes; two downward arrows mark beats that come sooner than expected with no wave just before them.

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
set2.q: A 76-year-old man develops atrial fibrillation. What is happening in his atria?
opts: Many sites fire chaotically
Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregular electrical activity of multiple sites within the atria, which suppresses the sinoatrial node.
One reentry loop circulates
A single reentry circuit, usually in the right atrium, is atrial flutter; fibrillation is many sites firing chaotically.
Three foci take turns
Three competing foci with distinct P waves is a wandering pacemaker or multifocal atrial tachycardia.
The sinus node fires faster
In fibrillation the sinus node is suppressed, not speeded up; chaotic atrial sites take over.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 32

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set2.q: A 47-year-old man's strip shows an early narrow beat. Which feature marks it as a premature atrial complex?
opts: No P wave and a wide QRS
A wide early beat with no P wave is a premature ventricular complex.
An early P wave of new shape
Correct. Premature atrial complexes arrive early in the cardiac cycle with P waves of different morphology, followed by a narrow QRS.
An inverted P with short PR
An inverted P wave with a short PR points to the atrioventricular junction, a premature junctional complex.
A late beat after a pause
A late beat after a pause is an escape beat; a premature atrial complex arrives early.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 6

set2.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set2.q: A 55-year-old woman's lead II strip is shown. What pattern do her premature beats follow?
opts: Bigeminy
Bigeminy is a premature beat every other beat; here two normal beats come between each early one.
Quadrigeminy
Quadrigeminy places three normal beats before each early one; here there are two.
A triplet
A triplet is three premature beats in a row; here single early beats recur every third beat.
Trigeminy
Correct. Every third beat is a premature complex, two normal beats then an early one, repeating: trigeminy.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 9
set2.alt: Lead II strip with narrow complexes in repeating groups of three, the third of each group arriving early.

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman's strip is shown; every wide premature beat has the same shape. What does the matching shape indicate?
opts: One ectopic focus
Correct. Premature ventricular complexes with the same morphology are unifocal, coming from the same ectopic focus.
Several ectopic foci
Several foci produce premature ventricular complexes of differing shapes, which is multifocal.
An atrial origin
An atrial beat is narrow with its own P wave; these wide beats are ventricular, all from one focus.
A junctional origin
A junctional beat is narrow; matching wide beats come from a single ventricular focus.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 70, 71
set2.alt: Strip of narrow beats interrupted twice by runs of tall broad complexes that all look alike, a run of four and a run of three.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set2.q: A 74-year-old woman's rate is 50 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm also lacks P waves, but its complexes are wide and its rate is 20 to 40.
Junctional escape rhythm
Correct. A regular narrow-complex rhythm of 40 to 60 per minute with no visible P waves is a junctional escape rhythm; the P waves are hidden or absent.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia would show an upright P wave before each QRS; here there are none.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is the same pattern over 100 per minute; at 50 it is an escape rhythm.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 54, 57, 58
set2.alt: Rhythm strip on dark grid paper with regularly spaced narrow complexes and no wave in front of them.

set2.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
set2.q: A 77-year-old man's strip shows a narrow junctional beat. How does a junctional escape beat differ in timing from a premature junctional complex?
opts: It comes early, before the next R
Arriving early defines the premature junctional complex; the escape beat comes late.
It falls every other beat
Every other beat describes bigeminy, a pattern of premature beats; an escape beat follows a pause.
It comes late, after a pause
Correct. A junctional escape beat comes late, past where the next R wave was expected; a premature junctional complex comes early.
It lands on the T wave
A beat on the T wave is the R on T danger of a premature ventricular complex; escape beats come late.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 50, 52

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
set2.q: A 30-year-old man has typical atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. How does the circuit travel?
opts: Down the slow tract, up the fast
Correct. In the typical form the circuit travels counterclockwise down the slow tract and up the fast tract; P waves are absent or buried at the end of the QRS.
Down the fast tract, up the slow
Down the fast and up the slow is the atypical form, in which retrograde P waves are clearly visible.
Around the right atrium
A circuit around the right atrium is atrial flutter, which produces a sawtooth baseline.
Through Bachmann's bundle
Bachmann's bundle carries impulses between the atria; the reentry circuit uses the slow and fast tracts.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 39

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set2.q: An 83-year-old man's rate is 40 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
Junctional escape rhythms are typically narrow, from the atrioventricular node; these complexes are wide.
Sinus arrest
Sinus arrest is a long flat gap in a sinus rhythm; this is a steady, slow, wide rhythm.
Idioventricular rhythm
Correct. Regular, wide complexes with opposite-direction T waves, no P waves and a rate of 20 to 40 per minute make idioventricular rhythm.
Premature ventricular complexes
Premature ventricular complexes interrupt an underlying rhythm early; here every beat is wide and evenly spaced.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 76, 79, 80
set2.alt: Strip with four widely spaced broad complexes, each followed by an opposite-direction wave, flat baseline between.

set2.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
set2.q: A 28-year-old woman has sudden palpitations; her rate is 200 per minute (normal 60 to 100). What is the rhythm on her strip?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia shows a distinct upright P wave before each QRS; here no separate P wave can be picked out between the complexes.
Supraventricular tachycardia
Correct. A regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves at 150 to 300 per minute is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, commonly called supraventricular tachycardia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with P waves of three shapes; this rhythm is perfectly regular.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular; these complexes are evenly spaced.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 38, 40, 41, 42
set2.alt: Blue grid strip of very rapid, evenly spaced narrow complexes; after each one the trace climbs to a single pointed wave that falls straight into the next complex.

set2.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
set2.q: A 60-year-old man's rate is 60 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia has the same three-shape P waves but runs over 100 per minute; at 60 it is a wandering atrial pacemaker.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia is irregular too, but every P wave has the same sinus shape; here the P waves change shape.
Wandering atrial pacemaker
Correct. The rhythm is irregular, under 100 per minute, with P waves of at least three different shapes still married to the QRS: a wandering atrial pacemaker.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation has no P waves at all, only fibrillatory waves; here distinct P waves precede every QRS.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 11, 12, 13, 14
set2.alt: Pink grid strip of narrow complexes at slightly uneven spacing; the small waves before them vary in shape.

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
set2.q: A 26-year-old woman's strip is shown; her rate jumps abruptly from about 100 to about 200 per minute (normal 60 to 100). What kind of beat usually sets off this reentry tachycardia?
opts: A ventricular escape beat
An escape beat arrives late after nodal failure; the reentry tachycardia is usually started by an early atrial ectopic beat.
A dropped sinus cycle
A dropped cycle is sinus exit block; a narrow-complex reentry tachycardia usually starts with a premature atrial complex.
A junctional escape beat
Junctional escape beats come late after the sinus node fails; the usual trigger is an early atrial beat.
A premature atrial complex
Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is usually set off by an ectopic beat, typically a premature atrial complex near the fast or slow tract.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 38
set2.alt: Pink grid strip labeled 100 bpm on the left and 200 bpm on the right; regular narrow complexes abruptly become twice as frequent.

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman has atrial flutter. Which atrial change sets up its circuit?
opts: A hypersensitive sinus node
Sinus node problems give sinus pauses, arrest or exit block; flutter arises from enlarged, scarred or ischemic atrium.
An extra internodal tract
The internodal tracts are normal anatomy; flutter's circuit is set up by enlarged, scarred or ischemic tissue.
High vagal tone
Vagal tone changes the sinus rate, as in sinus arrhythmia; flutter comes from enlarged or scarred atrial tissue.
Enlarged or scarred atrial tissue
Correct. The flutter reentry circuit is caused by chamber enlargement or by scarred or ischemic tissue.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 23

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman's strip shows no P waves in atrial fibrillation. What replaces them?
opts: Flutter waves
Flutter waves form the organized sawtooth of atrial flutter; fibrillation shows disorganized fibrillatory waves.
Inverted P waves
Inverted P waves come from a junctional impulse; fibrillation has fibrillatory waves instead of P waves.
Retrograde P waves
Retrograde P waves follow the QRS in junctional beats and reentry tachycardia; fibrillation shows fibrillatory waves.
Fibrillatory waves
Correct. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves; fibrillatory (f) waves are present instead, and the atrial rate is indeterminate.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 33, 35, 37

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
set2.q: A 72-year-old man has an irregular narrow-complex tachycardia. Which finding favors multifocal atrial tachycardia over atrial fibrillation?
opts: An irregularly irregular rhythm
Irregularly irregular is the defining regularity of atrial fibrillation; both rhythms are irregular.
A rate over 100 per minute
Both rhythms can run over 100 per minute; distinct P waves of three shapes point to multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Narrow QRS complexes
Both are supraventricular and can have narrow complexes; the three P wave shapes are the distinguishing finding.
P waves of three distinct shapes
Correct. Multifocal atrial tachycardia has visible P waves of at least three morphologies married to the QRS; atrial fibrillation has no P waves, only fibrillatory waves.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 18, 33

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
set2.q: A 62-year-old man's flutter circuit is mapped. Where does it most often run?
opts: The right atrium
Correct. The reentry circuit of atrial flutter most often occurs in the right atrium.
The left atrium
The left atrium can be involved, but flutter's reentry circuit most often runs in the right atrium.
The atrioventricular node
A reentry circuit over the slow and fast pathways near the node is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia; flutter runs in the right atrium.
The left ventricle
Flutter is an atrial rhythm; its reentry circuit is in the right atrium, not the ventricles.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 23

set2.io: Compare and contrast junctional and idioventricular rhythms
set2.q: A 75-year-old man has a regular rhythm at 30 per minute (normal 60 to 100) with no P waves. Which pacemaker is most likely in control?
opts: The atrioventricular node
The atrioventricular node's intrinsic rate is 40 to 60 per minute; 30 is below it, in the Purkinje range.
The Purkinje network
Correct. A rate of 20 to 40 per minute is the Purkinje network's intrinsic rate, the rate of idioventricular rhythm.
The sinoatrial node
The sinus node runs 60 to 100 per minute with upright P waves; this is slower and has none.
An atrial focus
An atrial focus would produce P waves; this slow rhythm has none and runs at the Purkinje rate.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 76

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set2.q: A 59-year-old man's rate is 80 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Accelerated junctional rhythm
Correct. A regular junctional rhythm (inverted P waves, short PR, narrow QRS) at 60 to 100 per minute is an accelerated junctional rhythm.
Junctional escape rhythm
A junctional escape rhythm is 40 to 60 per minute; at 80 the junctional rhythm is accelerated.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is over 100 per minute; 80 falls in the accelerated range.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm has upright P waves and a normal PR; inverted P waves with a short PR are junctional.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 59, 60, 61
set2.alt: Pink grid strip with regularly spaced narrow complexes, each with a small deflection close in front of it.

set2.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
set2.q: A 68-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation has a chaotic, shapeless baseline and an irregularly irregular rhythm; this baseline is an organized sawtooth.
Atrial flutter
Correct. The baseline between the narrow QRS complexes is a continuous sawtooth of flutter waves, a pattern pathognomonic of atrial flutter.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia shows separate P waves of three shapes; here the baseline is a repeating sawtooth.
Wandering atrial pacemaker
A wandering atrial pacemaker shows distinct P waves of several shapes under 100 per minute, not a sawtooth.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 24, 26, 27
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with three-second tick marks: narrow complexes separated by a continuous zigzag baseline of repeating pointed waves.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set2.q: A 51-year-old woman's rate is 120 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her lead II strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia shows upright P waves in lead II; inverted P waves with a short PR are junctional.
Junctional escape rhythm
A junctional escape rhythm is 40 to 60 per minute; at 120 it is junctional tachycardia.
Atrial flutter
Atrial flutter replaces P waves with a sawtooth baseline; here each QRS has a single inverted P.
Junctional tachycardia
Correct. Inverted P waves just before narrow QRS complexes, a short PR and a regular rate of 120 make junctional tachycardia (over 100).
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 64, 67, 68
set2.alt: Lead II strip with closely spaced narrow complexes, each with a small downward deflection just before it.

set2.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set2.q: A 68-year-old man's lead II strip is shown. What pattern do the wide premature beats follow?
opts: Bigeminy
Bigeminy is a premature beat every other beat; here three normal beats separate the wide ones.
Trigeminy
Trigeminy is every third beat premature; here it is every fourth.
Quadrigeminy
Correct. Every fourth beat is a wide premature complex, three normal beats then an early one: quadrigeminy (here ventricular).
A couplet
A couplet is two wide beats back to back; here each wide beat stands alone, every fourth beat.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 10, 73
set2.alt: Lead II strip with narrow complexes and, at regular intervals, a single broad deep complex after every three narrow ones.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
set2.q: A 71-year-old woman's strip is shown; her narrow-complex rhythm has no visible P waves. What explains their absence?
opts: The atria fire first
Atria firing first would leave an inverted P wave before the QRS; here there is none.
The sinus node is firing
A sinus-driven rhythm shows upright P waves; their absence points to a junctional impulse.
Atria and ventricles fire together
Correct. When a junctional impulse depolarizes the atria and ventricles at the same time, the QRS hides the P wave (or the atria are never depolarized).
The impulse starts in the ventricle
A ventricular rhythm would be wide; these complexes are narrow, junctional with the P hidden.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 48
set2.alt: Rhythm strip of regularly spaced narrow complexes, each followed by a rounded wave, with flat baseline and no wave before them.

set2.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
set2.q: A 64-year-old woman's strip is shown. Where do the wide premature beats arise?
opts: In the atria
Atrial premature beats are narrow with an early P wave of new shape; these beats are wide.
In the junction
Junctional beats are usually narrow; these early beats are broad and bizarre.
In the ventricles
Correct. The wide, abnormal early beats with opposite-direction T waves are premature ventricular complexes, here recurring every third beat (trigeminy).
In the sinus node
Sinus beats are the narrow ones with normal P waves; the wide beats come from the ventricles.
set2.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 69, 73
set2.alt: Strip framed in orange: two narrow beats then one broad beat, repeating across the strip.
